templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, your {lead} quickly gives you instructions with three parts. You understood the first and third parts, but you are unsure about the second. Your {lead} is still standing next to you.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Repeat the instructions back in your own words and ask about the part you are unsure of.
options.why: Paraphrasing shows what you understood and exposes any gaps, and asking right away while your {lead} is there prevents a mistake later.

options.text: Nod and start working, then figure out the second part as you go along.
options.why: Guessing at an unclear part risks doing the work wrong. A quick question costs less than redoing it.
options.misconception: Asking a question makes me look unprepared.

options.text: Wait until later and ask a coworker instead, so you do not take up more of your {lead}'s time.
options.why: A coworker may not know exactly what your {lead} meant, and asking now takes seconds while your {lead} is right there.
options.misconception: Asking a coworker is always less bothersome than asking the supervisor.

options.text: Say you understood everything and plan to ask for the instructions in writing if needed later.
options.why: Saying you understood when you did not leaves your {lead} unaware of the gap, and it may only come to light after a mistake.
options.misconception: Saying I understand is polite even when I do not.

templates.principle: Confirm what you heard by repeating it in your own words and ask about anything unclear while the speaker is still available.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a} who knows little about the technical side of the work asks why {deliverable|the} is delayed. The cause involves several technical steps that took longer than expected.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Explain the delay in plain language, give the new timing, and ask whether they have questions.
options.why: Matching your words to what the listener knows makes the message usable. Giving the new timing and inviting questions confirms they understood.

options.text: Use the exact technical terms for each step so that the explanation is as precise as possible.
options.why: Precise terms only help a listener who knows them. If the listener cannot follow the words, the message has not been communicated.
options.misconception: More technical detail makes an explanation better.

options.text: Send a long written explanation covering every step in detail so that nothing is left out.
options.why: Too much detail buries the main point. A listener who wants to know about the delay needs the reason and the new timing, not every step.
options.misconception: The more complete the explanation, the better.

options.text: Tell them it is delayed and that you cannot go into details, then move on to the next task.
options.why: A very short answer leaves the person without a reason or a new date, and it can sound dismissive even if the details are complicated.
options.misconception: A short answer saves everyone time.

templates.principle: Fit your message to the listener: use plain words, give the key point and what happens next, and check for questions.

templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, you assign {coworker} a new part of {task|the}. {coworker} says, "Sure, that is fine," but looks away, crosses {coworker}'s arms, and gives short answers when you ask questions. A few minutes later, you have a chance to talk with {coworker} alone.

options.text: Check in privately, say what you noticed, and ask whether anything about the new assignment is a concern.
options.why: Words and body language do not match, so asking openly and privately gives the person room to share a concern that they did not voice in the moment.

options.text: Take "that is fine" at face value and continue, since that is what was said out loud.
options.why: Words are only part of a message. When body language suggests otherwise, a quick check can prevent a problem from growing.
options.misconception: What someone says is the only part that counts.

options.text: Tell {coworker} in front of the group that {coworker} looks upset and ask what the problem is.
options.why: Calling out someone's reaction in front of others can embarrass them and make them less likely to open up. A private check is more respectful.
options.misconception: Raising it publicly shows I am paying attention.

options.text: Ask other coworkers whether they know why {coworker} seems unhappy with the new assignment.
options.why: Asking others puts the person's feelings into circulation without their consent and does not give them a chance to speak for themselves.
options.misconception: Other people will know the reason better than the person.

templates.principle: When words and body language do not match, check in privately and ask rather than assuming or discussing the person with others.
templates.timing: A private moment exists now; the first action is to use it to check in.

templates.scenario: A coworker practices this phone greeting before answering calls for {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that would not work with a caller.

segments.whyFine: A courteous opening that identifies the workplace.
Giving your name helps the caller know who is helping.

segments.text: Hold on, I am busy right now, so what do you want?
segments.why: This sounds impatient and dismissive. Callers expect a welcoming tone and an offer to help.

segments.text: How can I help you today?
segments.whyFine: An open, friendly offer to help is what a caller wants to hear.

templates.principle: Speak to your audience's needs: a welcoming tone and clear offer to help matter as much as the words themselves.

review.notes: Single line with a dismissive tone.

templates.scenario: Your {lead} asks you to give a short update to the team at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Put these preparation steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Decide the main message your audience needs
Organize your points in a clear order
Give the update and invite questions

precedence.why: You cannot organize points until you know the main message.
Practice works best on a clear structure.
Practicing before the update helps you present smoothly.

templates.principle: Prepare a presentation by choosing your message, organizing it, practicing, and then delivering it with time for questions.

templates.scenario: You are giving a short update to a team at {workplace|the}. Halfway through, several listeners look confused, one is frowning at the handout, and another whispers to a neighbor. You have ten minutes left of your time.

options.text: Pause, ask what part is unclear, and explain it again with a simpler example before continuing.
options.why: Listeners' expressions are telling you the message is not landing. Pausing to check and simplifying fixes it while there is still time.

options.text: Keep going so that you finish on time, and invite questions at the very end.
options.why: Inviting questions at the end is good, but by then confused listeners may have lost the rest of the message.
options.misconception: The plan I prepared is the plan I should follow.

options.text: Speak faster and more loudly so that people stop whispering and pay attention.
options.why: Speaking faster usually makes things harder to follow, and the whispering may be about the confusion, not rudeness.
options.misconception: Confusion means people are not listening.

options.text: Skip ahead to your conclusion so that the talk ends sooner and nobody is bored.
options.why: Skipping the middle leaves listeners without the information they need, and the confusion remains unaddressed.
options.misconception: Shorter is always better when people look lost.

templates.principle: Watch your audience while speaking; when they look lost, pause and adjust instead of pressing on.

review.notes: Acceptable option is orderly but late.
